claims.text: A controlled silver addition introduced by alloying or surface treatment will remain available for thermally and mechanically driven migration during sliding.
Silver will segregate to grain boundaries during sliding.
Silver will migrate to the sliding surface during sliding.
Localized silver segregation will form a thin, continuous silver-rich lubricious film.
Sliding-induced heating and plastic deformation drive silver diffusion toward high-stress grain boundaries and surfaces.
The segregated silver-rich material forms a low-shear-strength phase.
A deformable lubricious interfacial layer can promote smoother, lower-friction sliding.
The silver-rich interfacial layer reduces adhesive interactions and direct metal-to-metal contact.
The silver-rich interfacial layer suppresses localized plastic deformation.
Silver modification will lower the steady-state coefficient of friction relative to an untreated HEA under identical conditions.
Silver modification will lower the wear rate relative to an untreated HEA under identical conditions.
The reductions in friction and wear will persist from room temperature through elevated service temperatures.
An untreated CoCrFeNi-based HEA typically relies on oxide-film formation for its friction and wear behavior.
Intrinsic microstructural heterogeneities contribute to the untreated HEA's friction and wear behavior.
The beneficial effect will persist only while the silver content remains below levels that produce deleterious bulk precipitates.
Excessive silver addition can compromise the alloy's core mechanical properties.
At sufficiently high temperatures, excessive silver diffusion may deplete silver from critical interfacial regions and reduce the lubricating effect.
Rapid oxidation may override the proposed silver-lubrication mechanism.
